items.title: When Assam Villages Went Underwater, These Rescuers Crossed Raging Floods to Bring Families Home
items.blurb: The night the waters rose, roads disappeared first. Paths that villagers had walked for years vanished beneath muddy currents. Homes that once held laughter, meals, and memories slowly filled with floodwater . For many families across Upper Assam, the only way out was no longer through the familiar roads but across the dangerous waters that had swallowed them. And then came the boats. As floodwaters surrounded villages in Jorhat, Sivasagar and Golaghat, rescue teams moved through the submerged landscape, taking people away from danger while giving frightened families a reason to believe they would be safe again. They carried hope to families waiting in darkness, unsure of when help would arrive. Behind every boat crossing the flooded rivers was a story of courage, patience, and a promise that no one would be left behind. According to The Assam Tribune , teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), Civil Defence, district disaster management teams, Fire and Emergency Services, Assam Police and local volunteers worked continuously to evacuate stranded residents and provide relief to communities cut off by the floods. Racing against rising waters For rescue personnel, every minute mattered. When distress calls began arriving on the night of 19 July, NDRF teams stationed in Jorhat immediately began preparing for operations. Kuldeep Sharma, second-in-command of the 1st Battalion NDRF, said the teams had been receiving emergency calls as villages began going underwater and their priority was reaching people before conditions became more dangerous. They also helped move patients from a hospital inside the Teok tea estate, including a newborn baby who was only 20 days old. Photograph: (Instagram @ndrfindia) The rescuers navigated through unpredictable currents, damaged roads and rapidly changing water levels. They reached homes that had been cut off by the floods, helping families escape the rising waters while also rushing patients to safety when every moment mattered. Among the most challenging missions was the rescue operation in Kawaimari Mising village in Teok, where road connectivity had been completely cut off. Acting on information from the District Disaster Management Authority, the NDRF team travelled several kilometres by boat to reach an elderly woman who needed immediate evacuation. In another operation, rescuers reached villagers who were dangerously surrounded by rising waters. They also helped move patients from a hospital inside the Teok tea estate, including a newborn baby who was only 20 days old. For the teams on the ground, every rescue had a face, a family and a story behind it. The boats that became lifelines When villages go underwater, a boat becomes more than a means of transport. It becomes a bridge between fear and safety. Elderly residents who could not walk through deep water, children held tightly by worried parents, pregnant women, and people battling illness all depended on these rescue boats. The teams worked through difficult conditions, mostly travelling through areas where the strength of the current made navigation risky. However, with each journey, they brought people closer to dry land and temporary safety. The SDRF remained deployed alongside other agencies, carrying out evacuations during the early days of the flood. As water levels began to fall in some areas, their role expanded from rescue operations to distributing relief materials and supporting rehabilitation efforts. The rescue continued For many, falling water levels might appear to signal the end of the crisis. For rescue teams, however, the challenges did not stop. As floodwaters receded, boats that once moved easily through deep waters began facing new difficulties in shallow areas. Breached embankments and damaged roads made it harder for vehicles carrying food, medicines and emergency supplies to reach isolated villages. When villages go underwater, a boat becomes more than a means of transport. Photograph: (Instagram @ndrfindia) The rescue effort was no longer just about pulling people out of danger. It was about helping communities begin again. Teams delivered essential supplies, assisted vulnerable residents and remained prepared for fresh emergencies because another spell of heavy rain could drastically change the situation. The people behind the lifelines The impact of a flood is usually counted in numbers , as villages affected, people taken to safety and relief camps opened. But numbers cannot show what it feels like to leave behind a home, watch familiar places disappear under water and depend on the kindness of strangers during the hardest moments. Behind those figures are moments of humanity. A rescuer reaching out a hand to an elderly villager stepping into a boat. A family leaving behind a flooded home but carrying the hope of returning someday. A medical patient being carefully transported through water because reaching a hospital could mean the difference between life and death. According to flood reports cited by The Assam Tribune , hundreds of villages and thousands of people remained affected, with relief camps and distribution centres continuing to support those displaced by the disaster. The floodwaters may have covered roads, fields and homes, but they could not erase the determination of those who entered the waters to help. While many watched the rivers rise, these rescuers moved towards the danger. The teams worked through difficult conditions, mostly travelling through areas where the strength of the current made navigation risky. They stepped into boats, faced uncertain currents , and crossed flooded villages because, for the families waiting on the other side, they were not just rescue workers. They were the people bringing them home.

items.title: At This Howrah Sweet Shop, the Family Legacy Runs From Mother to Daughter
items.blurb: This shop looks like any other neighbourhood sweet seller on Netaji Subhash Road in Howrah. Whitewashed walls, a squeaking ceiling fan, wooden benches and a glass case stacked with kalakand and milk cake. But what stops most visitors in their tracks is the signboard above the door: Ghosal & Daughter. A name that plays tricks on assumption At first glance, the name can evoke a familiar picture: a father running the business with the daughter who may inherit it one day. Across India, business names ending in “& Sons” have made male succession feel familiar. Ghosal & Daughter carries a different story. Sutapa Ghosal founded the shop herself in 2018 and hopes to pass it on to her daughter, Momoiro Mukherjee. The business begins with a mother and may one day continue through her daughter. From newsreader to sweet maker Before she ever thought of selling sweets , Sutapa Ghosal worked as an announcer and television host with Doordarshan. She also holds a PhD in drama from Rabindra Bharati University, a background far removed from the world of syrup and chhena. When she decided to enter the food business , she returned to the classroom. Sutapa pursued a degree in food processing from Jadavpur University before opening her shop in Howrah. Milk cake and kalakand are close cousins in Indian confectionery, both built from concentrated, granulated milk rather than the smoother chhena used in Bengali sweets like sandesh. Her professional experience and academic qualifications did not shield her from the gendered assumptions she encountered as a woman building a business. "It doesn't matter who claims our society has overcome the traditional norms ; women endure the silent gaze of patriarchy even today. So it is an extra challenge for me to resist," she told My Kolkata. Starting without a recipe book to inherit Unlike many sweet shop owners who inherit both a trade and a network of skilled workers, Ghosal started with neither. "Being a sole entrepreneur in the sweet industry without a family business to inherit , one of the toughest challenges I face is finding skilled sweet makers. The reality for new business owners is difficult," she said. She now hires her staff largely from Nadia and Howrah, though she admits that maintaining consistent quality across batches remains an ongoing struggle, one that many independent food entrepreneurs quietly wrestle with as they scale up. Despite this, her kalakand and milk cake have earned her a loyal, returning clientele in a city already spoilt for choice when it comes to traditional sweets. The daughter who pushed her to begin It was Momoiro Mukherjee, in fact, who nudged her mother towards opening the shop in the first place. "My daughter has been my biggest support throughout my journey," Ghosal said. That support has now come full circle. The shop is not just named for Momoiro; it is meant, quite literally, to become hers. A legacy passed from mother to daughter Family businesses in India have long carried an unspoken script: a father builds, a son or a brother inherits, and a daughter, if she is involved at all, plays a supporting role. West Bengal has the highest share of women-owned MSMEs of any Indian state, at over 23 percent, official survey data shows, a backdrop that makes Howrah fertile ground for shops like this one. Ghosal & Daughter turns that script on its head without ever raising its voice. There is no dramatic declaration on the signboard, only a simple pairing of a mother's name with her daughter's place in the story. For Sutapa Ghosal, that pairing is not incidental. It is a deliberate, everyday assertion that businesses, dreams and legacies do not need a patriarch's blessing to move forward. They can travel from mother to daughter with the same ease, the same pride and the same sense of continuity that has traditionally been reserved for sons. Eight years since it first opened its doors, Ghosal & Daughter continues to serve fresh sweets to its regulars in Howrah. But every time a customer glances up at that signboard and pauses, if only for a second, to question who really built this shop, the sweet shop is doing something rather more significant than selling kalakand. It is quietly challenging an assumption most people did not even realise they were making. items.title: Why Parents Around the World Are Looking to India’s Tradition of Sleeping Beside Kids
items.blurb: Can you remember the first night you slept in a room of your own? Or did that moment never really come until you were much older? For many Indians, childhood nights weren't spent alone. They meant squeezing into the family bed, listening to bedtime stories, drifting off to the sound of a grandmother's lullaby, or instinctively reaching for a parent's hand in the middle of the night. While many Western cultures have long celebrated independent sleeping as a milestone of growing up, India has quietly held on to a different philosophy — one where sleeping together is simply another way of expressing love and care. Now, interestingly, this age-old parenting practice is finding renewed global attention as researchers, anthropologists and parents revisit what co-sleeping really means. And they're discovering something surprising: co-sleeping isn't unusual at all. In fact, studies suggest nearly two-thirds of the world's population practises some form of co-sleeping, making solitary sleep a cultural norm in only certain parts of the world rather than a universal parenting practice. More than sharing a bed Co-sleeping broadly refers to parents and children sleeping in close proximity. It can mean bed-sharing, where a baby sleeps on the same sleep surface as the parents, or room-sharing, where the baby sleeps in a separate crib or bassinet in the parents' room. Co-sleeping remains deeply rooted in many Asian cultures, where family closeness is seen as an important part of a child's early years. Photograph: ( The Mulberry Bush ) Across much of India, co-sleeping has never really been a parenting "trend". It has simply been the default. From practical reasons like shared living spaces to easier nighttime breastfeeding and a culture that places immense value on family closeness, generations have grown up believing babies belong close to their caregivers — even while they sleep. In fact, studies estimate that between 60% and 90% of families across many Asian countries, including India, Japan and China, practise co-sleeping in some form. Unlike many Western societies that encourage children to sleep independently from an early age, Indian parenting has traditionally viewed nighttime proximity as an extension of caregiving rather than a habit that needs to be broken. The practice reflects a broader Indian philosophy of family life, where interdependence is often valued over early independence. Sleep, much like meals and festivals, becomes another experience the family shares. Why the world is looking again For decades, parenting advice across much of North America and Europe promoted separate nurseries and independent sleep routines. But that conversation is becoming more nuanced. Anthropologists argue that humans have rarely slept alone throughout history. In fact, researchers suggest our species spent over 95% of its evolutionary history sleeping alongside family members or communities, where shared sleep offered warmth, protection and opportunities for caregiving. From that perspective, separate bedrooms for infants are actually a fairly recent cultural invention. As parenting conversations evolve worldwide, traditional practices like co-sleeping are being revisited through the lens of attachment and responsive caregiving. Photograph: ( Masilo ) This shift in thinking is prompting researchers to examine co-sleeping beyond the lens of convenience. New conversations now explore its role in attachment, emotional security, responsive parenting and breastfeeding. Social media has also amplified discussions around attachment parenting, with parents across Europe and North America increasingly questioning whether independence must begin in infancy. The benefits and the important caveats Parents who practise co-sleeping often describe it as instinctive. Sleeping nearby allows caregivers to respond quickly to feeding cues, comfort a crying baby within moments and maintain close physical contact through the night. Experts also point out that room-sharing can make breastfeeding easier. Since the World Health Organisation recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, having a baby close by often helps mothers feed more responsively without fully waking or moving between rooms. But experts are equally clear that cultural acceptance should never overshadow safety. Experts say that while sleeping close to a child can strengthen caregiver-child bonds, safe sleep practices should always remain a priority. Photograph: ( Education World ) Medical professionals warn that bed-sharing with newborns can increase the risk of suffocation and other sleep-related infant deaths if safe sleep practices are not followed. The risks become significantly higher if parents smoke, consume alcohol, take sedative medication, sleep on sofas or very soft mattresses, or if the baby is premature or has a low birth weight. This is why many paediatricians recommend room-sharing without bed-sharing during a baby's early months. In fact, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that infants sleep in the parents' room on a separate, firm sleep surface for at least the first six months, ideally the first year, noting that room-sharing can reduce the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) by up to 50%. The message isn't to reject tradition — it's to practise it safely. A parenting practice rooted in connection Perhaps the growing interest in co-sleeping isn't really about where a child sleeps. It's about recognising that there isn't one universal blueprint for raising children. For Indian families, co-sleeping has long been woven into everyday life rather than consciously chosen. What once seemed like an ordinary household routine is now becoming part of a much larger global conversation about attachment, responsive caregiving and emotional wellbeing. India's long-standing tradition of co-sleeping is contributing to a global conversation about emotional wellbeing, connection, and the many ways children feel secure. Photograph: (Ai generated) As parenting philosophies continue to evolve, India's centuries-old bedtime tradition is reminding the world that closeness and independence don't have to be opposites. Sometimes, the strongest sense of security begins with simply knowing that someone is right there beside you. Whether families choose to co-sleep or not, one thing remains constant: children thrive when they feel safe, loved and supported. And perhaps that's the real lesson this age-old practice has to offer. Source: 'The Truth About Co-Sleeping: Prevalence, Statistics, Benefits, and Risks' by Raskana. items.title: Behind the Scenes Of A Rescue Operation That Guides Royal Bengal Tigers From A Village to The Wild
items.blurb: Three men sit shoulder to shoulder inside a narrow wooden patrol boat as it moves through a winding creek in the Sundarbans. Sheets of monsoon rain blur the mangroves behind them as they patrol one of the many waterways that separate villages from the Sundarbans tiger habitat. Speaking to The Better India from the middle of the creek during one such patrol, the men keep scanning both banks on the sides. On one side of the creek lies a cluster of homes protected by nylon fencing. And across the water begins the tiger's world. The distance between them is barely a few dozen metres. Actually so small that, during low tide, it appears almost walkable. " Nodir opare bagh, epare amra, thakte toh hobei ekshathe" ( The tiger lives on that side of the river. We live on this side. We have to coexist)," says Pintu Mondal, a member of the Primary Response Team (PRT) of the Wildlife Trust of India(WTI), speaking to The Better India as the boat continues its patrol through the rain. He watches the opposite bank and smiles. In the Sundarbans, that coexistence is practically a daily operation. But a decade or two ago, if a tiger entered a village, the first reaction would have been how not to get killed, or how to kill the tiger before it killed someone else. A landscape where rivers decide everything The Sundarbans Delta stretches across nearly 10,000 sq km of India and Bangladesh, making it one of the world's largest contiguous mangrove ecosystems and one of the highest-priority Tiger Conservation Units globally. Around 40 percent of the delta lies in India, while the remaining mangroves are in Bangladesh. The landscape is threaded together by hundreds of rivers, creeks, and estuaries formed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna river systems. This is also home to the largest single population of Royal Bengal tigers . Rescuing injured or trapped big cats requires close contact in swampy, low-visibility tidal environments where tigers are powerful swimmers and adept stalkers. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust Of India) On the Indian side alone, the 2022 All India Tiger Estimation recorded an estimated 101 tigers with a density of 4.27 tigers per 100 sq km. But these are not the tigers most people imagine. They are smaller than their mainland counterparts, with adult males typically weighing between 97 and 115 kilograms. Generations of living in saline marshes have shaped them into powerful swimmers capable of crossing tidal rivers with ease. Their coats often appear darker and glossier. So, what makes a tiger rescue in the Sundarbans so different from almost every other rescue operation? "For us, these rivers are roads. For the tigers too, these are roads.", Pintu Mondal answers. And that changes everything. In the world's largest mangrove forest, the only mangrove habitat of the Royal Bengal tiger, there are no forest tracks to follow, no dry ground to chase across. Here, a tiger can swim across a creek with the tide and find itself in the middle of a village. To understand what really happens next, The Better India sat down with the people behind these rescues, reconstructing — minute by minute — what it takes to guide a tiger safely back home. Minute 1: Someone spots the pugmarks The first sign may be fresh pugmarks outside a cowshed. Dogs barking before sunrise. Someone returning from the field spots movement near a bamboo grove. Word spreads. The village informs the Forest Department. The police are alerted. Members of the Primary Response Team (PRT), trained local volunteers supported through Wildlife Trust of India (WTI), and other such organisations begin moving towards the location. At this point, everyone knows the first objective, which is simply to guide the tiger back into the forest. Minute 30: The exits are planned before anyone moves The Sundarbans cannot be treated like a mainland forest. Every creek, embankment, and mudflat changes with the tide. "If the tiger has entered from the river, we don't close that side," Samrat Paul, Field Officer for WTI's Sundarban Tiger Project, explains. "If we push it from the village, it should have an option to swim back." Instead, teams begin covering possible escape routes leading deeper into human settlements while intentionally leaving the forest-facing direction open." Finding fresh tiger pug marks is common during a Sundarbans National Park safari, while direct tiger sightings are rare. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust Of India) In the Sundarbans, tranquilisation is rare," says Samrat. "The terrain itself makes every decision more complicated, so the rescue is designed around the tiger's instinct to retreat.” Minute 60 (in rare cases): The village becomes part of the rescue Many imagine wildlife rescues as specialists arriving with cages and dart guns. In reality, the first attempt involves no chemicals, just coordinated pressure. The first objective is always to give the tiger a chance to leave on its own," explains Samrat, who assists the West Bengal Forest Department and the WTI's Rapid Response Teams to safely capture and guide stray tigers back into the depths of the Sundarban Tiger Reserve (STR). Villagers and trained responders position themselves at safe distances while the Forest Department coordinates the operation. Drums are beaten in a steady pattern in synchrony to create a wall of sound that gradually nudges the tiger away from human habitation. Firecrackers, locally known as potka , burst, and after dark, powerful lights are switched on. "The idea isn't to terrify the animal," Paul says. "It's to make the village feel unfamiliar and uncomfortable, while keeping the route back to the forest open. A tiger naturally prefers the security of dense cover, so if it has a safe exit, it will choose to return." These non-lethal methods are the first line of response recommended by wildlife experts because they encourage the tiger to leave on its own, reducing the need for capture and lowering the risk for both people and the animal. Most rescues end here. The tiger slips back into the mangroves. Minute 120: When the tiger refuses to leave Sometimes, it doesn't. It hides inside thick vegetation, or settles in a paddy field, or moves further inland. Only then do response teams prepare for the next phase: Nets. The nets used are unlike fishing nets. They are heavy-gauge barriers, often layered twice or three times, designed to gently funnel the tiger towards a safe enclosure or transport crate. If even that fails, the Forest Department may deploy a steel-reinforced cage fitted with an automatic closing mechanism. A live bait, usually a goat, may be used under carefully monitored conditions . Even at this point, the aim remains temporary containment before the tiger is released back into suitable habitat. Chemical immobilisation is considered only in exceptional situations. Why does a tiger enter a village? Why a tiger crosses into a village isn't always easy to explain. "There isn't enough scientific evidence to point to one single reason for tiger straying in the Sundarbans," says Samrat. "People often assume it's because the animal is hungry, but we can't conclusively say that. It could be territorial movement, pressure from another dominant tiger, or even movement during the breeding season. Every incident is different." Sometimes, he says, the landscape itself is responsible. "From the opposite bank, a tiger doesn't necessarily see a village. The riverbanks are lined with mangroves and trees, so what looks like a settlement to us may simply appear as another stretch of forest to the tiger. It swims across, thinking it is entering more habitat, and only after crossing does it encounter houses, livestock, and people." Unlike elephants, which move in herds guided by older matriarchs who pass on knowledge of safe routes, "A tiger is solitary. It doesn't have that kind of inherited road map. It isn't following another tiger that already knows the landscape." There have been rare exceptions. Samrat Paul recalls a radio-collared tiger from around 2008–09 that repeatedly returned to the same area near Pakhiralay despite being relocated. "It kept coming back to the same landscape," he says. "Eventually, after repeated straying incidents, the decision was taken to translocate it to a zoo. But those are exceptional cases." The rescue that lasted a week Not every rescue ends within hours. Pintu Mondal remembers one operation in the Kultali landscape that stretched across seven days. The tiger kept shifting through mangrove patches and muddy fields. As daylight faded, teams turned to drones to look for signs of movement above the dense vegetation. "At night, drones helped us scan areas that would have been impossible to search on foot," Mondal explains. "Meanwhile, our boats kept changing position with the tides because the waterways here are constantly changing. You have to work with the landscape, not against it." Despite days of tracking, the tiger never entered the cage. And that, Mondal says, was not a failure. "In the end, it found its own way back to the forest. That is always the best outcome. If a tiger returns on its own, it means there is less stress for the animal and much less risk for everyone involved." He says that such outcomes are more common than people realise. "In 2025, around the Kultali block alone, we recorded 37 incidents of tigers straying into villages. Only two eventually had to be captured. In almost every other case, the tigers went back on their own." Then he points to what has changed the most over the years. "We couldn't have managed those rescues without the villagers. Today, they cooperate with us, they inform us quickly, and they help us keep people away from the animal instead of chasing it." Rapid coastal erosion, rising sea levels, and unpredictable cyclone surges continually shrink the safe working zones and disrupt mangrove stability. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust Of India) One of the biggest reasons rescue operations look different today is the network of Primary Response Teams (PRTs), better known locally as Baghbondhu or "Friends of the Tiger". Unlike outside rescue personnel, these volunteers belong to the very villages where these conflicts happen. "The idea behind Baghbondhu is a local feeling," Samrat Paul explains. "Organisations like ours can support the landscape, but we won't always be there. The people who live here are the ones who will respond first. So we wanted to build a system where the community itself knows what to do when a tiger enters a village." For the Baghbondhus , the role goes far beyond emergency response. They help maintain fencing, assist the Govt Forest Department during rescues, respond to calls involving snakes and other wildlife, and spend much of the year speaking to fellow villagers about how to react calmly when animals stray. "When the message comes from someone within your own community, people trust it more. They are our own people, naturally when someone from your own village explains what to do, people listen," Paul says. A rescue remembered for the wrong reasons Basudev Mondal, a 34-year-old Primary Response Team member on the boat, now opens up to The Better India . He still remembers a rescue from his teenage years. There were no trained community teams then, so he has witnessed that change firsthand. "Back then, we didn't have organised rescue nets or a proper system for handling these situations," he recalls. "For us, a tiger only meant one thing: danger. The first thought was never how to save it. It was how to save ourselves." “In fact, we grew up hearing one phrase all the time, ' Baghe khabe ', which is literally (the tiger will eat you)," he says. "Parents would say it whenever children wandered too far from home. 'Don't go there, ‘ baghe khabe. ' It became part of our childhood. The tiger was something we feared from the time we were little That day, a male tiger had strayed nearly six kilometres into their village before taking shelter in paddy fields. "As soon as people heard there was a tiger, crowds gathered from all directions," he says. "Everyone wanted to see it, but in doing so they surrounded the animal. Instead of leaving it an escape route, people unknowingly blocked every side." The Forest Department eventually reached the spot and prepared to tranquilise the tiger. "But the tiger was frightened," he says. "The moment the dart was fired, it charged towards the veterinarian, and both of them rolled and fell into the river." The chaos only escalated. "The tiger managed to get out and ran into a nearby house. It crawled under a bed because it was exhausted and had nowhere else to go," Basudev Mondal recalls. Eventually, forest staff managed to wrap the tiger in nets before placing it inside a transport cage. "But by then the damage had already been done," he says. "People had beaten it with sticks. Some even pulled out their whiskers. The tiger later died." Nylon net fences are physical barriers deployed along the fringes of the Sundarbans mangrove forest to prevent Royal Bengal tigers from straying into human settlements and to reduce human-tiger conflicts. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust Of India) For Basudev Mondal, that rescue marks how much attitudes have shifted over the years. "Back then, we didn't know why tigers were important," he says. "People acted out of fear because they didn't understand the animal." Today, he says, the response in many villages is almost unrecognisable. "Now, if someone spots a tiger, the first instinct is to inform the Forest Department or the Primary Response Team. Even when villagers find a snake or a turtle, they call us instead of trying to kill it.” Better rescue = fewer tiger attack deaths? It is important to distinguish between rescue operations and tiger attacks. Rescue operations come into play only when a tiger strays into a human settlement; they are distinct from the many human-tiger encounters that occur inside or along forest habitats during livelihoods such as fishing, crab collection, and honey harvesting. This reconstruction offers a glimpse into how a rescue operation unfolds when a tiger enters a village. But across the Sundarbans, many documented and undoubtedly undocumented human-tiger encounters continue to end in tragedy. So, rescue is only one part of reducing conflict. Preventing tigers from entering villages remains equally important. Kultali remains among the blocks most affected by human-tiger interactions in the Indian Sundarbans. Data compiled by the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), an organisation working with the families of those killed or attacked by tigers in the Sundarbans reportedly recorded at least 10 human-tiger encounters this year until May, resulting in eight deaths and two injuries. For the teams who patrol these creeks, they are careful not to suggest that rescue operations can prevent every human-tiger encounter. Conflicts and fatal attacks can still occur in a landscape where people live inside or along the tiger habitat. What a rescue operation can do is prevent a tiger that has already strayed into a village from becoming the centre of another tragedy. By calming crowds, creating a safe escape route and coordinating with the Forest Department, the teams work to reduce the risk to both people and the animal. All pictures and videos by : Wildlife Trust Of India

items.title: Cristina Kirchner expands her international legal team to take the Vialidad case abroad
items.blurb: Former Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner has added Brazilian jurist Rafael Valim to the team preparing a filing before international bodies to challenge her conviction in the Vialidad case, according to sources close to her cited by the Argentine press. items.blurb: Argentine President Javier Milei on Saturday endorsed the presidential candidacy of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro at the Liberal Party (PL) National Convention in São Paulo, in a speech with sharp criticism of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva that drew rejection from Brazil's governing party and a response from the judiciary.
